text: Chapter 12: Might I Have a Bit of Earth?
Mary ran so fast that she was quite out of breath by the time she reached her room.
Her hair was messy on her forehead and her cheeks were bright pink. Her dinner was waiting on the table, and Martha was standing nearby.
Mary said in a determined voice.
Martha looked rather taken aback, but she looked pleased, too.
hes the best boy that was ever born, but we never thought he was handsome. His nose turns up too much.
I like it to turn up,
And his eyes are so round,
Though they are a nice color.
And they are exactly the color of the sky over the moor.
Mother says his eyes became that color because hes always looking up at the birds and the clouds. But he has a big mouth, doesnt he?
I wish mine was just like it.
It would look very funny on your tiny face,
But I knew youd like him when you saw him. How did you like the seeds and the garden tools?
How did you know he brought them?
Oh, I never doubted hed bring them. Hed be sure to bring them if they were to be found in Yorkshire. Hes such a trustworthy boy.

Mary was afraid that Martha might begin to ask difficult questions, but she didnt. Martha was very interested in the seeds and gardening tools, and there was only one moment when Mary was frightened. This was when Martha asked where the flowers were going to be planted.
Who did you ask about it?
Well, I wouldnt ask the head gardener. Hes too grand, Mr. Roach is.
Ive only seen the assistant gardeners and Ben Weatherstaff.
If I were you, Id ask Ben Weatherstaff,

Hes not half as bad as he looks, even though hes so grumpy. Mr. Craven lets him do what he likes because he was here when Mrs. Craven was alive, and he used to make her laugh. She liked him. Perhaps hed find you a corner somewhere out of the way.
If it was out of the way and no one wanted it, no one could mind my having it, could they?
There wouldnt be any reason not to,
Mary ate her dinner as quickly as she could. When she got up from the table, she was about to run to her room to put on her hat again, but Martha stopped her.
Ive got something to tell you,
I thought Id let you eat your dinner first. Mr. Craven came back this morning, and I think he wants to see you.
Why? He didnt want to see me when I first arrived. I heard Pitcher say he didnt.

Mrs. Medlock says its because of my mother. She was walking to Thwaite village and met him. Shed never spoken to him before, but Mrs. Craven had been to our cottage two or three times. He had forgotten, but mother hadnt, and she was brave enough to stop him. I dont know what she said to him about you, but she said something that made him decide to see you before he goes away again tomorrow.
Is he going away tomorrow? I am so glad!
Hes going away for a long time. He might not come back until autumn or winter. Hes going to travel to foreign places. Hes always doing that.

If he did not come back until winter, or even autumn, there would be time to watch the secret garden come alive. Even if he found out about it then and took it away from her, she would have had that much at least.
When do you think he will want to see—

She did not finish the sentence because the door opened and Mrs. Medlock walked in. She was wearing her best black dress and cap, and her collar was fastened with a large brooch featuring a mans face. It was a colored photograph of Mr. Medlock, who had died years ago, and she always wore it when she was dressed up. She looked nervous and excited.
Go and brush it. Martha, help her slip on her best dress. Mr. Craven sent me to bring her to his study.

All the color left Marys cheeks. Her heart began to thump, and she felt herself changing back into a stiff, plain, silent child. She did not even answer Mrs. Medlock, but turned and walked into her bedroom, followed by Martha. She said nothing while her dress was changed and her hair was brushed. Once she was tidy, she followed Mrs. Medlock down the corridors in silence. What was there for her to say? She had to go and see Mr. Craven, and he would not like her, and she would not like him. She knew what he would think of her.
She was taken to a part of the house she had not visited before. At last, Mrs. Medlock knocked at a door, and when someone said,
they entered the room together. A man was sitting in an armchair before the fire, and Mrs. Medlock spoke to him.
You can leave her here. I will ring for you when I want you to take her away,

After she left and closed the door, Mary could only stand waiting, a plain little thing, twisting her thin hands together. She could see that the man in the chair was not so much a hunchback as a man with high, rather crooked shoulders, and his black hair was streaked with white. He turned his head over his high shoulders and spoke to her.

He was not ugly. His face would have been handsome if it had not looked so miserable. He looked as if the sight of her worried and troubled him, and as if he did not know what in the world to do with her.
Do they take good care of you?
He rubbed his forehead fretfully as he looked her over.
Mary answered in what she knew was her stiffest tone.
What an unhappy face he had! His black eyes seemed as if they scarcely saw her, as if they were looking at something else, and he could hardly keep his attention on her.
How could I remember? I intended to send you a governess or a nurse, or someone like that, but I forgot.
and then the lump in her throat choked her.
What do you want to say?
I am—I am too big for a nurse,
And please—please dont make me have a governess yet.
He rubbed his forehead again and stared at her.
That was what the Sowerby woman said,
Then Mary gathered a bit of courage.
What do you want to do?
Mary answered, hoping her voice would not tremble.
I never liked playing outside in India. But it makes me hungry here, and I am getting fatter.
Mrs. Sowerby said it would do you good. Perhaps it will,
She thought you should get stronger before you have a governess.
It makes me feel strong when I play and the wind blows across the moor,
Marthas mother sent me a skipping rope. I skip and run, and I look around to see if things are beginning to sprout out of the earth. I dont do any harm.
he said in a worried voice.
A child like you couldnt do any harm! You may do whatever you like.
Mary put her hand to her throat because she was afraid he might see the lump of excitement she felt rising there. She took a step closer to him.
Her anxious little face seemed to worry him more than ever.

Of course you may. I am your guardian, though I am a poor one for any child. I cannot give you time or attention. I am too ill, miserable, and distracted, but I want you to be happy and comfortable. I dont know anything about children, but Mrs. Medlock will make sure you have everything you need. I sent for you today because Mrs. Sowerby said I should see you. Her daughter had talked about you, and she thought you needed fresh air, freedom, and running around.
Mary said again, in spite of herself.
I thought she was rather bold to stop me on the moor, but she said my wife had been kind to her.
It seemed hard for him to say his late wifes name.

She is a respectable woman. Now that I have seen you, I think she made a lot of sense. Play outdoors as much as you like. Its a large estate, and you may go wherever you like and amuse yourself however you like. Is there anything you want?
he asked, as if a sudden thought had struck him.
Do you want toys, books, or dolls?
might I have a bit of earth?
In her eagerness, she did not realize how strange those words sounded or that they were not the ones she had meant to say. Mr. Craven looked quite startled.
To plant seeds in—to make things grow—to see them come alive,
He gazed at her for a moment and then passed his hand quickly over his eyes.
Do you care about gardens that much?
I didnt know about them in India,
I was always sick and tired, and it was too hot. Sometimes I made little garden beds in the sand and stuck flowers in them. But here, it is different.
Mr. Craven got up and began to walk slowly across the room.
he said to himself, and Mary thought that she must have reminded him of something. When he stopped and spoke to her, his dark eyes looked almost soft and kind.
You can have as much earth as you want,
You remind me of someone else who loved the earth and things that grow. When you find a bit of earth that you want,
he added with a slight smile,
take it, child, and make it come alive.
May I take it from anywhere—if no one else wants it?
There, you must go now. I am tired.
He rang the bell to call Mrs. Medlock.
Goodbye. I shall be away all summer.
Mrs. Medlock arrived so quickly that Mary thought she must have been waiting in the corridor.

now that I have seen the child, I understand what Mrs. Sowerby meant. She needs to become stronger before she begins her lessons. Give her simple, healthy food. Let her run wild in the garden. Dont supervise her too closely. She needs freedom, fresh air, and outdoor play. Mrs. Sowerby is to come and see her now and then, and Mary may sometimes visit their cottage.

Mrs. Medlock looked pleased. She was relieved to hear that she did not have to supervise Mary too closely. She had found the girl to be a tiresome responsibility and had indeed seen as little of her as she could. In addition, she was very fond of Marthas mother.

Susan Sowerby and I went to school together, and shes as sensible and good-hearted a woman as you could find anywhere. I never had any children myself, and shes had twelve, and there were never healthier or better-behaved kids. Miss Mary will come to no harm with them. I would always take Susan Sowerbys advice about children myself. Shes what you might call healthy-minded, if you understand what I mean.
Take Miss Mary away now and send Pitcher to me.
When Mrs. Medlock left her at the end of her own corridor, Mary flew back to her room. She found Martha waiting there. In fact, Martha had hurried back right after clearing the dinner table.

I may have it wherever I like! I am not going to have a governess for a long time! Your mother is coming to see me, and I can go to your cottage! He says a little girl like me couldnt do any harm, and I can do whatever I like—anywhere!
That was nice of him, wasnt it?
he is really a nice man, but his face is so sad and his forehead is all wrinkled up.

She ran as quickly as she could to the garden. She had been away much longer than she expected, and she knew Dickon would have to set out early on his five-mile walk home. When she slipped through the door under the ivy, she saw he was not working where she had left him. The gardening tools were laid together under a tree. She ran to them, looking all around the place, but Dickon was nowhere to be seen. He had gone, and the secret garden was empty—except for the robin, who had just flown over the wall and sat on a rosebush, watching her.
Oh, was he—was he only a forest fairy?

Something white fastened to the rosebush caught her eye. It was a piece of paper—in fact, a piece of the letter she had printed for Martha to send to him. It was pinned to the bush with a long thorn, and Mary knew instantly that Dickon had left it there. There were some roughly printed letters on it and a simple drawing. At first, she couldnt tell what it was. Then she saw it was meant to be a nest with a bird sitting on it. Underneath were the printed letters, which read:
